name: Nero d’Avola

lines.s10: Nero d'Avola is Sicily's own red, deep and generous, with black cherry and liquorice on a soft, round tannin.
lines.s20: Nero d'Avola is the red grape of Sicily, named for the town of Avola near Syracuse. It pours deep and ripe, with black cherry, mulberry and liquorice, a full body and gentle tannin that suit grilled meat and tomato.
lines.s45: In Sicily, Nero d'Avola is the red on every table, grown across the island and most at home in the south east. It is deep in colour, with black cherry, mulberry and a touch of liquorice. The body is full and the tannin soft and round. Much of it is bottled young for that fruit, while wines from Pachino and Noto, on limestone by the sea, are firmer and keep longer. Pour it beside pasta with aubergine and tomato, grilled sausage or lamb chops. Growers in Australia's warm, dry regions have taken it up for the way it copes with the heat.
lines.sale: Nero d'Avola pours the warmth of Sicily with no hard edge: ripe black cherry and liquorice on soft tannin. Bring it when the table shares grilled sausage and a pasta with aubergine.

glass.lead: Black cherry, black plum and mulberry with liquorice, deep ruby and full, on a soft, round tannin.

ladder.where: The high inland hills of Contea di Sclafani
Vittoria, Noto and Pachino, the west of Sicily, the Riverland

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium and round, alcohol medium plus to high, body medium plus to full; deep ruby to purple.

home.home: Sicily, all over the island, with the south east around Vittoria, Noto and Pachino at its heart. Since 2017 a bottle that names the grape must be a DOC, most often Sicilia DOC. With Frappato it makes Cerasuolo di Vittoria, the island's one DOCG.
home.abroad: Australia has taken it up for the way it copes with heat and drought, above all in McLaren Vale and the Riverland, and makes it as a bright, fruit led red.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; Cerasuolo di Vittoria a shade cooler.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass for a full Nero d'Avola; a Burgundy bowl for perfumed Cerasuolo di Vittoria.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a young, soft bottle; an older or oaked one may open with a short decant.
service.age: Most within two to five years; a structured bottle from Pachino or Noto can keep longer.

with.dish: Pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and tomato
with.why: ripe, soft fruit meets sweet tomato and aubergine
soft tannin and dark fruit for fat and fennel
ripe fruit and a round grip for charred meat

with.dish: Seared tuna, with Cerasuolo di Vittoria
with.why: a lighter red with soft tannin for meaty fish

labels.means: The island wide DOC, and since the 2017 vintage the usual home of a bottle that names Nero d'Avola.
Sicily's one DOCG: Nero d'Avola, 50 to 70 per cent, with Frappato. A red, not a rosé.
An older Sicilian name for Nero d'Avola, still met on some labels.
DOCs of the south eastern tip near Syracuse, where Nero d'Avola grows on limestone by the sea.
The island's IGT; since 2017 it may not print Nero d'Avola on the label.

guest.a: A small town on the coast south of Syracuse, in the south east of Sicily, that gave the grape its name. The wine comes from all over the island.
A cousin in spirit: deep, ripe and generous. Nero d'Avola is softer and rounder, with gentler tannin, and without Shiraz's pepper and smoked meat.

guest.q: Will a red work with the tuna?
guest.a: A light one will. Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Nero d'Avola with Frappato, brings strawberry, perfume and soft tannin that sit well with a meaty fish.

compare.tell: Syrah carries cracked black pepper, black olive and smoked meat over firmer tannin; Nero d'Avola has none of the meat or olive, and a softer, rounder grip.
Nerello Mascalese, from Etna, is pale and high in acidity, with sour cherry and volcanic ash; Nero d'Avola is deep in colour, softer and rounder, with mulberry and liquorice.
Aglianico grips far harder, with high acidity, tar and smoke; Nero d'Avola is softer and rounder, with mulberry and liquorice.

profile.st: Deep ruby to purple · Body medium plus to full · Acid medium · Tannin medium, soft and round · Alcohol medium plus to high · Dry
profile.fruit: Black cherry, black plum, mulberry; prune and dried fig from hot sites
profile.other: Liquorice, tobacco leaf and leather; dark chocolate and vanilla from new oak; a soft, round texture
profile.tell: Deep colour and ripe black cherry, plum and mulberry with liquorice, on soft, round tannin and a full body
profile.regions: Sicily: Vittoria, Noto and Pachino in the south east, the west and the interior hills; McLaren Vale and the Riverland in Australia
profile.confuse: Syrah carries pepper, black olive and smoked meat; Nerello Mascalese is pale and high in acid; Aglianico grips far harder

cards.front: Nero d'Avola: where does its name come from, and what is its older name?
cards.back: Avola, a small town near Syracuse in the south east of Sicily. Its older Sicilian name is Calabrese.

cards.front: Cerasuolo di Vittoria: which grapes, in what shares, and what colour?
cards.back: Nero d'Avola, 50 to 70 per cent, with Frappato, 30 to 50: a red, not a rosé, and Sicily's one DOCG, since 2005.

cards.front: Nero d'Avola on a label: what has the 2017 vintage changed?
cards.back: Terre Siciliane IGT may no longer print Nero d'Avola or Grillo. A bottle that names either must be a DOC, most often Sicilia DOC, or a local one such as Noto or Vittoria.

questions.q: A red poured blind is deep ruby, with black cherry, mulberry and liquorice, soft, round tannin and a full body. The guest says it comes from a Mediterranean island. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour and ripe black cherry and mulberry on soft, round tannin point to Nero d'Avola. Nerello Mascalese, the nearest miss and Sicilian too, is pale, with sour cherry and high acidity.

questions.q: A guest wants a Sicilian red that still holds Nero d'Avola but is lighter and more perfumed than a varietal bottle. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Cerasuolo di Vittoria blends Nero d'Avola with 30 to 50 per cent Frappato, which brings strawberry, perfume and lift. Etna Rosso, the nearest miss, is lighter too but is Nerello Mascalese.

questions.q: A guest sees Calabrese on the back label of a Sicilian red and asks which grape that is. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Calabrese is an older Sicilian name for Nero d'Avola. Gaglioppo, the nearest miss, is the red grape of Calabria itself, the grape of Cirò.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; a thin grape, so the entry gives the profile. The Codex holds no TASTE row for it.

Cerasuolo di Vittoria (Nero d'Avola 50 to 70 per cent with Frappato 30 to 50, DOC 1973, DOCG 2005, the island's only DOCG), Sicilia DOC of 2011 and its 2017 reservation of varietal Nero d'Avola and Grillo, Avola as a town and not an appellation, Calabrese as the old name, Pachino and Noto on limestone giving the most structured wines, Contea di Sclafani cooling it with altitude, and tuna, sausage with fennel and aubergine and tomato dishes all stand on the Codex's Sicily record and INTRO_GRAPES.

Mulberry, liquorice, tobacco and leather rest on trade tasting guides read through search; acidity is given as medium, as INTRO_GRAPES has it, though Australian growers prize the grape for keeping its freshness in heat.

INTRO_GRAPES gives the aroma as Black cherry, plum, liquorice, spice: the bare family word spice is the kind the table names (here liquorice and cinnamon). The Codex's Sicily record calls it the island's most planted red, a volatile fact the entry leaves out.

Abroad: McLaren Vale and the Riverland stand on Wine Companion, Decanter, Wine Selectors and the Codex's Australia record; heat and drought tolerance on trade pages and an Australian research document read through search. The hosts could not be opened in this session.
